I know very well that <hi type="italic">he who sent me is true,</hi> and will stand by me, and bear me out, for <hi type="italic">I speak to the world</hi> (to which I am sent as an ambassador) <hi type="italic">those things,</hi> all those and those only, <hi type="italic">which I have heard of him.</hi>" Here, <div eID="gen27349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27350" type="x-p"/> [1.] He suppresses his accusation of them. He had <hi type="italic">many things</hi> to charge them with, and many evidences to produce against them; but for the present he had said enough. Note, Whatever discoveries of sin are made to us, he that searches the heart has still more to judge of us, <reference osisRef="1John.3.20">1 John iii. 20</reference>. How much soever God reckons with sinners in this world there is still a further reckoning yet behind, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.34">Deut. xxxii. 34</reference>. Let us learn hence not to be forward to say all we can say, even against the worst of men; we may have many things to say, by way of censure, which yet it is better to leave <hi type="italic">unsaid,</hi> for what is it to us? <div eID="gen27350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27351" type="x-p"/> [2.] He enters his appeal against them to his Father: <hi type="italic">He that sent me.</hi> Here two things comfort him:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> That he had been <hi type="italic">true to his Father,</hi> and to the trust reposed in him: <hi type="italic">I speak to the world</hi> (for his gospel was to be preached to every creature) <hi type="italic">those things which I have heard of him.</hi> Being given for a <hi type="italic">witness to the people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.4">Isa. lv. 4</reference>), he was <hi type="italic">Amen,</hi> a <hi type="italic">faithful witness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.14">Rev. iii. 14</reference>. He did not <hi type="italic">conceal</hi> his doctrine, but spoke it <hi type="italic">to the world</hi> (being of common concern, it was to be of common notice); nor did he change or alter it, nor vary from the instructions he received from him that sent him. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That his Father would be <hi type="italic">true to him;</hi> true to the promise that he would <hi type="italic">make his mouth like a sharp sword;</hi> true to his purpose concerning him, which was a <hi type="italic">decree</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.7">Ps. ii. 7</reference>); true to the threatenings of his wrath against those that should reject him. Though he should not <hi type="italic">accuse</hi> them to his Father, yet the Father, who sent him, would undoubtedly reckon with them, and would be <hi type="italic">true</hi> to what he had said (<reference osisRef="Deut.18.19">Deut. xviii. 19</reference>), that whosoever would not hearken to that prophet whom God would raise up <hi type="italic">he would require it of him.</hi> Christ would not accuse them; "for," saith he, "he that sent me is true, and will pass judgment on them, though I should not demand judgment against them." Thus, when he <hi type="italic">lets fall</hi> the present prosecution, he <hi type="italic">binds them over</hi> to the judgment-day, when it will be too late to dispute what they will not now be persuaded to believe. <hi type="italic">I, as a deaf man, heard not; for thou wilt hear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.38.13">Ps. xxxviii. 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.15">15</reference>. Upon this part of our Saviour's discourse the evangelist has a melancholy remark (<reference osisRef="John.8.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">They understood not that he spoke to them of the Father.</hi> See here, 1. The power of Satan to blind the minds of those who believe not. Though Christ spoke so plainly of God as his Father in heaven, yet they did not understand whom he meant, but thought he spoke of some father he had in Galilee. Thus the plainest things are riddles and parables to those who are resolved to hold fast their prejudices; day and night are alike to the blind. 2. The reason why the threatenings of the word make so little impression upon the minds of sinners; it is because they understand not whose the wrath is that is revealed in them. When Christ told them of the truth of him that sent him, as a warning to them to prepare for his judgment, which is <hi type="italic">according to truth,</hi> they slighted the warning, because they understood not to whose judgment it was that they made themselves obnoxious. <div eID="gen27351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27352" type="x-p"/> (3.) He refers them to <hi type="italic">their own convictions</hi> hereafter, <reference osisRef="John.8.28-John.8.29">v. 28, 29</reference>. He finds they will not understand him, and therefore adjourns the trial till further evidence should come in; they that <hi type="italic">will not see shall see,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.26.11">Isa. xxvi. 11</reference>. Now observe here, <div eID="gen27352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27353" type="x-p"/> [1.] <hi type="italic">What</hi> they should ere long be <hi type="italic">convinced of: "You shall know that I am he,</hi> that Jesus is the true Messiah. Whether you will own it or no before men, you shall be made to know it in your own consciences, the convictions of which, though you may <hi type="italic">stifle,</hi> yet you cannot <hi type="italic">baffle: that I am he,</hi> not that you represent me to be, but he that I preach myself to be, he that should come!" Two things they should be convinced of, in order to this:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> That he did nothing <hi type="italic">of himself,</hi> not of himself as man, of himself alone, of himself without the Father, with whom he was <hi type="italic">one.</hi> He does not hereby derogate from his own inherent power, but only denies their charge against him as a <hi type="italic">false prophet;</hi> for of false prophets it is said that they prophesied <hi type="italic">out of their own hearts,</hi> and followed <hi type="italic">their own spirits. Secondly,</hi> That as <hi type="italic">his Father taught him</hi> so he <hi type="italic">spoke these things,</hi> that he was not <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">autodidaktos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">self-taught,</hi> but <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Theodidaktos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">taught of God.</hi> The doctrine he preached was the counterpart of the counsels of God, with which he was intimately acquainted; <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">kathos edidaxe, tauta lalo</hi></hi>—I speak those things, not only <hi type="italic">which</hi> he taught me, but <hi type="italic">as</hi> he taught me, with the same divine power and authority. <div eID="gen27353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27354" type="x-p"/> [2.] <hi type="italic">When</hi> they should be convinced of this: <hi type="italic">When you have lifted up the Son of man,</hi> lifted him up upon the cross, as the brazen serpent upon the pole (<reference osisRef="John.3.14">ch. iii. 14</reference>), as the sacrifices under the law (for Christ is the great sacrifice), which, when they were offered, were said to be <hi type="italic">elevated,</hi> or <hi type="italic">lifted up;</hi> hence the burnt-offerings, the most ancient and honourable of all, were called <hi type="italic">elevations</hi> (<hi type="italic">Gnoloth</hi> from <hi type="italic">Gnolah, asendit—he ascended</hi>), and in many other offerings they used the significant ceremony of <hi type="italic">heaving</hi> the sacrifice up, and <hi type="italic">moving</hi> it before the Lord; thus was Christ <hi type="italic">lifted up.</hi> Or the expression denotes that his death was his exaltation. They that put him to death thought thereby for ever to have <hi type="italic">sunk</hi> him and his interest, but it proved to be the advancement of both, <reference osisRef="John.12.24">ch. xii. 24</reference>. When the Son of man was <hi type="italic">crucified,</hi> the Son of man was <hi type="italic">glorified.</hi> Christ had called his dying his <hi type="italic">going away;</hi> here he calls it his being lifted <hi type="italic">up;</hi> thus the death of the saints, as it is their departure out of this world, so it is their advancement to a better. Observe, He speaks of those he is now talking with as the <hi type="italic">instruments</hi> of his death: when <hi type="italic">you have lifted up the Son of man;</hi> not that they were to be the <hi type="italic">priests</hi> to offer him up (no, that was his own act, he <hi type="italic">offered up himself</hi>), but they would be his betrayers and murderers; see <reference osisRef="Acts.2.23">Acts ii. 23</reference>. They <hi type="italic">lifted him up</hi> to the cross, but then he lifted up himself to his Father. Observe with what tenderness and mildness Christ here speaks to those who he certainly knew would put him to death, to teach us not to hate or seek the hurt of any, though we may have reason to think they hate us and seek our hurt. Now, Christ speaks of his death as that which would be a powerful conviction of the infidelity of the Jews. <hi type="italic">When you have lifted up the Son of man, then shall you know</hi> this. And why then? <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Because careless and unthinking people are often taught the worth of mercies by the want of them, <reference osisRef="Luke.17.22">Luke xvii. 22</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The guilt of their sin in putting Christ to death would so awaken their consciences that they would be put upon serious enquiries after a Saviour, and then would know that Jesus was he who alone could save them. And so it proved, when, being told that with wicked hands they had <hi type="italic">crucified and slain</hi> the Son of God, they cried out, <hi type="italic">What shall we do?</hi> and were made to know assuredly that this Jesus was <hi type="italic">Lord and Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.2.36">Acts ii. 36</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> There would be such signs and wonders attending his death, and the <hi type="italic">lifting of him up</hi> from death in his resurrection, as would give a stronger proof of his being the Messiah than any that had been yet given: and multitudes were hereby brought to believe that Jesus is the Christ, who had before contradicted and opposed him. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> By the death of Christ the pouring out of the Spirit was purchased, who would convince the world that <hi type="italic">Jesus is he,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.16.7-John.16.8">ch. xvi. 7, 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> The judgments which the Jews brought upon themselves, by putting Christ to death, which filled up the measure of their iniquity, were a sensible conviction to the most hardened among them that <hi type="italic">Jesus was he.</hi> Christ had often foretold that desolation as the just punishment of their invincible unbelief, and <hi type="italic">when it came to pass (lo, it did come</hi>) they could not but know that the great <hi type="italic">prophet had been among them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.33">Ezek. xxxiii. 33</reference>. <div eID="gen27354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27355" type="x-p"/> [3.] What supported our Lord Jesus in the mean time (<reference osisRef="John.8.29">v. 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that sent me is with me,</hi> in my whole undertaking; <hi type="italic">for the Father</hi> (the fountain and first spring of this affair, from whom as its great cause and author it is derived) <hi type="italic">hath not left me alone,</hi> to manage it myself, hath not deserted the business nor me in the prosecution of it, for <hi type="italic">do I always those things that please him.</hi> Here is, <div eID="gen27355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27356" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The assurance which Christ had of his Father's <hi type="italic">presence</hi> with him, which includes both a divine <hi type="italic">power</hi> going along with him to <hi type="italic">enable</hi> him for his work, and a divine <hi type="italic">favour</hi> manifested to him to <hi type="italic">encourage</hi> him in it. <hi type="italic">He that sent me is with me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Isa. xlii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.21">Ps. lxxxix. 21</reference>. This greatly <hi type="italic">emboldens</hi> our faith in Christ and our reliance upon his word that he had, and knew he had, his Father with him, to <hi type="italic">confirm the word of his servant,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.44.26">Isa. xliv. 26</reference>. The King of kings accompanied his own ambassador, to attest his mission and assist his management, and <hi type="italic">never left him alone,</hi> either solitary or weak; it also <hi type="italic">aggravated</hi> the wickedness of those that opposed him, and was an intimation to them of the <hi type="italic">premunire</hi> they ran themselves into by resisting him, for thereby they were found <hi type="italic">fighters against God.</hi> How easily soever they might think to crush him and run him down, let them know he had one to back him with whom it is the greatest madness that can be to <hi type="italic">contend.</hi> <div eID="gen27356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27357" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The ground of this assurance: <hi type="italic">For I do always those things that please him.</hi> That is, 1. That great affair in which our Lord Jesus was <hi type="italic">continually</hi> engaged was an affair which the <hi type="italic">Father that sent him</hi> was highly <hi type="italic">well pleased with.</hi> His whole undertaking is called the <hi type="italic">pleasure of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Isa. liii. 10</reference>), because of the counsels of the eternal mind about it, and the complacency of the eternal mind in it. 2. His management of that affair was in nothing <hi type="italic">displeasing</hi> to his Father; in executing his commission he punctually observed all his instructions, and did in nothing vary from them. No mere man since the fall could say such a word as this (for <hi type="italic">in many things we offend all</hi>) but our Lord Jesus never offended his Father in any thing, but, as became him, he <hi type="italic">fulfilled all righteousness.</hi> This was necessary to the validity and value of the sacrifice he was to offer up; for if he had in any thing <hi type="italic">displeased</hi> the Father himself, and so had had any sin of his own to answer for, the Father could not have been pleased with him as a propitiation for our sins; but such a priest and such a sacrifice became us as was perfectly pure and spotless. We may likewise learn hence that God's servants may <hi type="italic">then</hi> expect God's presence with them when they <hi type="italic">choose</hi> and do <hi type="italic">those things that please him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.66.4-Isa.66.5">Isa. lxvi. 4, 5</reference>. <div eID="gen27357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27358" type="x-p"/> V. Here is the good effect which this discourse of Christ's had upon some of his hearers (<reference osisRef="John.8.30">v. 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">As he spoke these words many believed on him.</hi> Note, 1. Though multitudes perish in their unbelief, yet there is a remnant according to the election of grace, who <hi type="italic">believe to the saving of the soul.</hi> If Israel, the whole body of the people, <hi type="italic">be not gathered,</hi> yet there are those of them in whom Christ will be <hi type="italic">glorious,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.49.5">Isa. xlix. 5</reference>. This the apostle insists upon, to reconcile the Jews' rejection with the <hi type="italic">promises made unto their fathers.</hi> There is a remnant, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.5">Rom. xi. 5</reference>. 2. The words of Christ, and particularly his <hi type="italic">threatening</hi> words, are made effectual by the grace of God to bring in poor souls to believe in him. When Christ told them that if they <hi type="italic">believed not</hi> they should <hi type="italic">die in their sins,</hi> and never get to heaven, they thought it was time to look about them, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.16">Rom. i. 16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.18">18</reference>. 3. Sometimes there is a <hi type="italic">wide door opened,</hi> and an <hi type="italic">effectual</hi> one, even where they are <hi type="italic">many adversaries.</hi> Christ will carry on his work, though <hi type="italic">the heathen rage.</hi> The gospel sometimes gains great victories where it meets with great opposition. Let this encourage God's ministers to preach the gospel, though it be with <hi type="italic">much contention,</hi> for they shall not <hi type="italic">labour in vain.</hi> Many may be <hi type="italic">secretly</hi> brought home to God by those endeavours which are openly contradicted and cavilled at by men of corrupt minds. Austin has an affectionate ejaculation in his lecture upon these words: <hi type="italic">Utinam et, me loquenti, multi credant; non in me, sed mecum in eo—I wish that when I speak, many may believe, not on me, but with me on him.</hi>
entries.55c6b97cb568fb1657958fac9a5877022b5f949a: <div eID="gen27358" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Discourse with the Pharisees.</title> <div sID="gen27359" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> Then said Jesus to those Jews which believed on him, If ye continue in my word, <hi type="italic">then</hi> are ye my disciples indeed; <hi type="super">32</hi> And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free. <hi type="super">33</hi> They answered him, We be Abraham's seed, and were never in bondage to any man: how sayest thou, Ye shall be made free? <hi type="super">34</hi> Jesus answered them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin. <hi type="super">35</hi> And the servant abideth not in the house for ever: <hi type="italic">but</hi> the Son abideth ever. <hi type="super">36</hi> If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed. <hi type="super">37</hi> I know that ye are Abraham's seed; but ye seek to kill me, because my word hath no place in you. <div eID="gen27359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27360" type="x-p"/> We have in these verses, <div eID="gen27360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27361" type="x-p"/> I. A comfortable doctrine laid down concerning the <hi type="italic">spiritual liberty</hi> of Christ's disciples, intended for the encouragement of <hi type="italic">those</hi> Jews <hi type="italic">that believed.</hi> Christ, knowing that his doctrine began to work upon some of his hearers, and perceiving that virtue had gone out of him, turned his discourse from the proud Pharisees, and addressed himself to those <hi type="italic">weak</hi> believers. When he had denounced wrath against those that were hardened in unbelief, then he spoke comfort to those few feeble <hi type="italic">Jews that believed in him.</hi> See here, <div eID="gen27361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27362" type="x-p"/> 1. How graciously the Lord Jesus looks to those that <hi type="italic">tremble at his word,</hi> and are ready to receive it; he has something to say to those who have hearing ears, and will not pass by those who set themselves in his way, without speaking to them. <div eID="gen27362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27363" type="x-p"/> 2. How carefully he cherishes the beginnings of grace, and meets those that are coming towards him. These <hi type="italic">Jews that believed</hi> were yet but <hi type="italic">weak;</hi> but Christ did not therefore cast them off, for he <hi type="italic">gathers the lambs in his arms.</hi> When faith is in its infancy, he has <hi type="italic">knees</hi> to <hi type="italic">prevent it, breasts</hi> for it to <hi type="italic">suck,</hi> that it may not <hi type="italic">die from the womb.</hi> In what he said to them, we have two things, which he saith to all that should at any time believe:— <div eID="gen27363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27364" type="x-p"/> (1.) The character of a true disciple of Christ: <hi type="italic">If you continue in my word, then are you my disciples indeed.</hi> When they <hi type="italic">believed on him,</hi> as the great prophet, they gave up themselves to be <hi type="italic">his disciples.</hi> Now, at their entrance into his school, he lays down this for a settled rule, that he would own none for his disciples but those that <hi type="italic">continued in his word.</hi> [1.] It is implied that there are many who profess themselves Christ's disciples who are not his <hi type="italic">disciples indeed,</hi> but only in show and name. [2.] It highly concerns those that are not <hi type="italic">strong in faith</hi> to see to it that they be <hi type="italic">sound in the faith,</hi> that, though not disciples of the highest form, they are nevertheless <hi type="italic">disciples indeed.</hi> [3.] Those who seem willing to be Christ's disciples ought to be told that they had as good never come to him, unless they come with a resolution by his grace to abide by him. Let those who have thoughts of covenanting with Christ have no thoughts of reserving a power of revocation. Children are sent to school, and bound apprentices, only for a <hi type="italic">few years;</hi> but those only are Christ's who are willing to be bound to him <hi type="italic">for the term of life.</hi> [4.] Those only that <hi type="italic">continue in Christ's word</hi> shall be accepted as his <hi type="italic">disciples indeed,</hi> that adhere to his word in every instance without partiality, and abide by it to the end without apostasy. It is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">menein</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">to dwell</hi> in Christ's word, as a man does at home, which is his centre, and rest, and refuge. Our converse with the word and conformity to it must be constant. If we continue disciples to the last, then, and not otherwise, we approve ourselves <hi type="italic">disciples indeed.</hi> <div eID="gen27364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27365" type="x-p"/> (2.) The privilege of a true disciple of Christ. Here are two precious promises made to those who thus approve themselves disciples indeed, <reference osisRef="John.8.32">v. 32</reference>. <div eID="gen27365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27366" type="x-p"/> [1.] "<hi type="italic">You shall know the truth,</hi> shall know all that truth which it is needful and profitable for you to know, and shall be more confirmed in the belief of it, shall know the certainty of it." Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Even those who are true believers, and disciples indeed, yet may be, and are, much in the dark concerning many things which they should know. God's children are but children, and understand and speak as children. Did we not need to be taught, we should not need to be disciples. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is a very great privilege to <hi type="italic">know the truth,</hi> to know the particular truths which we are to believe, in their mutual dependences and connections, and the grounds and reasons of our belief,—to know what is truth and what proves it to be so. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> It is a gracious promise of Christ, to all who continue in his word, that they shall know the truth as far as is needful and profitable for them. Christ's scholars are sure to be well taught. <div eID="gen27366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27367" type="x-p"/> [2.] <hi type="italic">The truth shall make you free;</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The truth which Christ teaches tends to make men free, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">Isa. lxi. 1</reference>. Justification makes us free from the guilt of sin, by which we were <hi type="italic">bound over</hi> to the judgment of God, and <hi type="italic">bound under</hi> amazing fears; sanctification makes us free from the bondage of corruption, by which we were <hi type="italic">restrained</hi> from that service which is perfect freedom, and <hi type="italic">constrained</hi> to that which is perfect slavery. Gospel truth frees us from the yoke of the ceremonial law, and the more grievous burdens of the traditions of the elders. It makes us <hi type="italic">free from</hi> our spiritual enemies, free <hi type="italic">in</hi> the service of God, free <hi type="italic">to</hi> the privileges of sons, and free <hi type="italic">of</hi> the Jerusalem which is from above, which is free. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The knowing, entertaining, and believing, of this truth does actually <hi type="italic">make us free,</hi> free from prejudices, mistakes, and false notions, than which nothing more <hi type="italic">enslaves</hi> and <hi type="italic">entangles</hi> the soul, free from the dominion of lust and passion; and restores the soul to the government of itself, by reducing it into obedience to its Creator. The mind, by admitting the truth of Christ in the light and power, is vastly enlarged, and has scope and compass given it, is greatly elevated and raised above things of sense, and never acts with so true a liberty as when it acts under a divine command, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.17">2 Cor. iii. 17</reference>. The enemies of Christianity pretend to <hi type="italic">free thinking,</hi> whereas really those are the freest reasonings that are guided by faith, and those are men of <hi type="italic">free thought</hi> whose thoughts are captivated and brought into obedience to Christ. <div eID="gen27367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27368" type="x-p"/> II. The offence which the carnal Jews took at this doctrine, and their objection against it. Though it was a doctrine that brought glad tidings of liberty to the captives, yet they cavilled at it, <reference osisRef="John.8.33">v. 33</reference>. The Pharisees grudged this comfortable word to those that believed, the standers by, who had <hi type="italic">no part nor lot in this matter;</hi> they thought themselves reflected upon and affronted by the gracious charter of liberty granted to those that believed, and therefore with a great deal of pride and envy they answered him, "<hi type="italic">We Jews are Abraham's seed,</hi> and therefore are <hi type="italic">free-born,</hi> and have not lost our birthright-freedom; <hi type="italic">we were never in bondage to any man; how sayest thou then,</hi> to us <hi type="italic">Jews, You shall be made free?</hi>" See here, <div eID="gen27368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27369" type="x-p"/> 1. What it was that they were grieved at; it was an <hi type="italic">innuendo</hi> in those words, <hi type="italic">You shall be made free,</hi> as if the Jewish church and nation were in some sort of bondage, which reflected on the Jews in general, and as if all that did not believe in Christ continued in that bondage, which reflected on the Pharisees in particular. Note, The privileges of the faithful are the envy and vexation of unbelievers, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.10">Ps. cxii. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen27369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27370" type="x-p"/> 2. What it was that they alleged against it; whereas Christ intimated that they needed to be made free, they urge, (1.) "We are Abraham's seed, and Abraham was a <hi type="italic">prince and a great man;</hi> though we live in Canaan, we are not descended from Canaan, nor under his doom, <hi type="italic">a servant of servants shall he be;</hi> we hold in <hi type="italic">frank-almoign—free alms,</hi> and not in <hi type="italic">villenage—by a servile tenure.</hi>" It is common for a sinking decaying family to boast of the glory and dignity of its ancestors, and to borrow honour from that name to which they repay disgrace; so the Jews here did. But this was not all. Abraham was in covenant with God, and his children by his right, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.28">Rom. xi. 28</reference>. Now that covenant, no doubt, was a free charter, and invested them with privileges not consistent with a state of slavery, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.4">Rom. ix. 4</reference>. And therefore they thought they had no occasion with so <hi type="italic">great a sum</hi> as they reckoned faith in Christ to be <hi type="italic">to obtain this freedom,</hi> when they were thus free-born. Note, It is the common fault and folly of those that have pious parentage and education to trust to their privilege and boast of it, as if it would atone for the want of real holiness. They were Abraham's seed, but what would this avail them, when we find one in hell that could call Abraham father? Saving benefits are not, like common privileges, conveyed by <hi type="italic">entail</hi> to us and our issue, nor can a title to heaven be made by <hi type="italic">descent,</hi> nor may we claim as <hi type="italic">heirs at law,</hi> by making out our pedigree; our title is purely by purchase, not our own but our Redeemer's for us, under certain provisos and limitations, which if we do not observe it will not avail us to be Abraham's seed. Thus many, when they are pressed with the necessity of regeneration, turn it off with this, <hi type="italic">We are the church's children;</hi> but they are not all Israel that are of Israel. (2.) <hi type="italic">We were never in bondage to any man.</hi> Now observe, [1.] How false this allegation was. I wonder how they could have the assurance to say a thing in the face of a congregation which was so notoriously <hi type="italic">untrue.</hi> Were not the seed of Abraham in bondage to the Egyptians? Were they not often in bondage to the neighbouring nations in the time of the judges? Were they not seventy years captives in Babylon? Nay, were they not at this time tributaries to the Romans, and, though not in a <hi type="italic">personal,</hi> yet in a <hi type="italic">national</hi> bondage to them, and groaning to be made free? And yet, to confront Christ, they have the impudence to say, <hi type="italic">We were never in bondage.</hi> Thus they would expose Christ to the ill-will both of the Jews, who were very jealous for the honour of their liberty, and of the Romans, who would not be thought to enslave the nations they conquered. [2.] How foolish the application was. Christ had spoken of a liberty wherewith the <hi type="italic">truth</hi> would make them free, which must be meant of a <hi type="italic">spiritual</hi> liberty, for truth as it is the <hi type="italic">enriching,</hi> so it is the <hi type="italic">enfranchising</hi> of the mind, and the <hi type="italic">enlarging</hi> of that from the captivity of error and prejudice; and yet they plead against the offer of <hi type="italic">spiritual</hi> liberty that they were never in <hi type="italic">corporal</hi> thraldom, as if, because they were never in bondage to any <hi type="italic">man,</hi> they were never in bondage to any <hi type="italic">lust.</hi> Note, Carnal hearts are sensible of no other grievances than those that molest the body and injure their secular affairs. Talk to them of encroachments upon their civil liberty and property,—tell them of waste committed upon their lands, or damage done to their houses,—and they understand you very well, and can give you a sensible answer; the thing touches them and affects them. But discourse to them of the bondage of sin, a captivity to Satan, and a liberty by Christ,—tell them of wrong done to their precious souls, and the hazard of their eternal welfare,—and <hi type="italic">you bring certain strange things to their ears;</hi> they say of it (as those did, <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.49">Ezek. xx. 49</reference>), <hi type="italic">Doth he not speak parables?</hi> This was much like the blunder Nicodemus made about being <hi type="italic">born again.</hi> <div eID="gen27370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27371" type="x-p"/> III. Our Saviour's vindication of his doctrine from these objections, and the further explication of it, <reference osisRef="John.8.34-John.8.37">v. 34-37</reference>, where he does these four things:— <div eID="gen27371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27372" type="x-p"/> 1. He shows that, notwithstanding their civil liberties and their visible church-membership, yet it was possible that they might be in a state of bondage (<reference osisRef="John.8.34">v. 34</reference>): <hi type="italic">Whosoever commits sin,</hi> though he be of Abraham's seed, and was never in bondage to any man, is the servant of sin. Observe, Christ does not upbraid them with the falsehood of their plea, or their present bondage, but further explains what he had said for their edification. Thus ministers should with meekness instruct those that oppose them, that they may <hi type="italic">recover themselves,</hi> not with passion provoke them to entangle themselves yet more. Now here, <div eID="gen27372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27373" type="x-p"/> (1.) The preface is very solemn: <hi type="italic">Verily, verily, I say unto you;</hi> an awful asseveration, which our Saviour often used, to command a reverent attention and a ready assent. The style of the prophets was, <hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord,</hi> for they were <hi type="italic">faithful as servants;</hi> but Christ, being a Son, speaks in his own name: <hi type="italic">I say unto you,</hi> I the <hi type="italic">Amen,</hi> the faithful witness; he pawns his veracity upon it. "I say it to you, who boast of your relation to Abraham, as if that would save you." <div eID="gen27373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27374" type="x-p"/> (2.) The truth is of universal concern, though here delivered upon a particular occasion: <hi type="italic">Whosoever commits sin is the servant of sin,</hi> and sadly needs to be made free. A state of sin is a state of bondage. [1.] See who it is on whom this brand is fastened—on him that <hi type="italic">commits sin,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pas ho poion hamartian</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">every one that makes sin.</hi> There is not a <hi type="italic">just man</hi> upon earth, that <hi type="italic">lives, and sins not;</hi> yet every one that sins is not a servant of sin, for then God would have no servants; but he that <hi type="italic">makes sin,</hi> that <hi type="italic">makes choice</hi> of sin, prefers the way of wickedness before the way of holiness (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.16-Jer.44.17">Jer. xliv. 16, 17</reference>),—that <hi type="italic">makes a covenant</hi> with sin, enters into league with it, and <hi type="italic">makes a marriage</hi> with it,—that <hi type="italic">makes contrivances</hi> of sin, <hi type="italic">makes provision</hi> for the flesh, and devises iniquity,—and that <hi type="italic">makes a custom</hi> of sin, who walks after the flesh, and <hi type="italic">makes a trade</hi> of sin. [2.] See what the brand is which Christ fastens upon those that thus <hi type="italic">commit sin.</hi> He stigmatizes them, gives them a mark of servitude. They are <hi type="italic">servants of sin,</hi> imprisoned under the guilt of sin, under an arrest, in hold for it, <hi type="italic">concluded under sin,</hi> and they are subject to the power of sin. He is a <hi type="italic">servant of sin,</hi> that is, he makes himself so, and is so accounted; he has <hi type="italic">sold himself to work wickedness;</hi> his lusts give law to him, he is at their beck, and is not his own master. He does the work of sin, supports its interest, and accepts its wages, <reference osisRef="Rom.6.16">Rom. vi. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen27374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27375" type="x-p"/> 2. He shows them that, being in a state of bondage, their having a place in the house of God would not entitle them to the inheritance of sons; for (<reference osisRef="John.8.35">v. 35</reference>) <hi type="italic">the servant,</hi> though he be in the house for awhile, yet, being but a <hi type="italic">servant, abideth not in the house for ever.</hi> Services (we say) are no inheritances, they are but <hi type="italic">temporary,</hi> and not for a <hi type="italic">perpetuity; but the son</hi> of the family abideth ever. Now, (1.) This points primarily at the rejection of the Jewish church and nation. Israel had been <hi type="italic">God's son,</hi> his <hi type="italic">first-born;</hi> but they wretchedly degenerated into a <hi type="italic">servile</hi> disposition, were enslaved to the world and the flesh, and therefore, though by virtue of their birthright they thought themselves secure of their church membership, Christ tells them that having thus made themselves servants they should not <hi type="italic">abide in the house for ever.</hi> Jerusalem, by opposing the gospel of Christ, which proclaimed liberty, and adhering to the Sinai-covenant, which gendered to bondage, after its term was <hi type="italic">expired</hi> came to be <hi type="italic">in bondage with her children</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.24-Gal.4.25">Gal. iv. 24, 25</reference>), and therefore was unchurched and disfranchised, her charter seized and taken away, and she was cast out as the son of the bond-woman, <reference osisRef="Gen.21.14">Gen. xxi. 14</reference>. Chrysostom gives this sense of this place: "Think not to be made free from sin by the rites and ceremonies of the law of Moses, for Moses was but a servant, and had not that perpetual authority in the church which the Son had; but, if the Son make you free, it is well," <reference osisRef="John.8.36">v. 36</reference>. But, (2.) It looks further, to the rejection of all that are the <hi type="italic">servants of sin,</hi> and receive not the <hi type="italic">adoption</hi> of the <hi type="italic">sons of God;</hi> though those unprofitable servants may be in God's house awhile, as retainers to his family, yet there is a day coming when the children of the <hi type="italic">bond-woman</hi> and of the <hi type="italic">free</hi> shall be distinguished. True believers only, who are the children of the promise and of the covenant, are accounted free, and shall abide for ever in the house, as Isaac: they shall have a <hi type="italic">nail</hi> in the holy place on earth (<reference osisRef="Ezra.9.8">Ezra ix. 8</reference>) and <hi type="italic">mansions</hi> in the holy place in heaven, <reference osisRef="John.14.2">ch. xiv. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen27375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27376" type="x-p"/> 3. He shows them the way of deliverance out of the state of bondage into the <hi type="italic">glorious liberty of the children of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.21">Rom. viii. 21</reference>. The case of those that are the servants of sin is sad, but thanks be to God it is not helpless, it is not hopeless. As it is the privilege of all the sons of the family, and their dignity above the servants, that they abide in the house for ever; so he who is <hi type="italic">the Son,</hi> the first-born among many brethren, and the heir of all things, has a power both of manumission and of adoption (<reference osisRef="John.8.36">v. 36</reference>): <hi type="italic">If the Son shall make you free, you shall be free indeed.</hi> Note, <div eID="gen27376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27377" type="x-p"/> (1.) Jesus Christ in the gospel offers us <hi type="italic">our freedom;</hi> he has authority and power to <hi type="italic">make free.</hi> [1.] To <hi type="italic">discharge prisoners;</hi> this he does <hi type="italic">in justification,</hi> by making satisfaction for <hi type="italic">our guilt</hi> (on which the gospel offer is grounded, which is to all a conditional <hi type="italic">act of indemnity,</hi> and to all true believers, upon their believing, an absolute <hi type="italic">charter of pardon</hi>), and for <hi type="italic">our debts,</hi> for which we were by the law arrested and in execution. Christ, as our surety, or rather our <hi type="italic">bail</hi> (for he was not originally bound <hi type="italic">with us,</hi> but upon our insolvency bound <hi type="italic">for us</hi>), compounds with the creditor, answers the demands of injured justice with more than an <hi type="italic">equivalent,</hi> takes the <hi type="italic">bond</hi> and <hi type="italic">judgment</hi> into his own hands, and gives them up <hi type="italic">cancelled</hi> to all that by faith and repentance give him (if I may so say) a <hi type="italic">counter-security</hi> to save his honour harmless, and so they are <hi type="italic">made free;</hi> and from the debt, and every part thereof, they are for ever acquitted, exonerated, and discharged, and a general release is sealed of all actions and claims; while against those who refuse to come up to these terms the securities lie still in the Redeemer's hands, in full force. [2.] He has a power to rescue <hi type="italic">bond-slaves,</hi> and this he does in <hi type="italic">sanctification;</hi> by the powerful arguments of his gospel, and the powerful operations of his Spirit, he breaks the power of corruption in the soul, rallies the scattered forces of reason and virtue, and fortifies God's interest against sin and Satan, and so the soul is made free. [3.] He has a power to <hi type="italic">naturalize strangers and foreigners,</hi> and this he does in <hi type="italic">adoption.</hi> This is a further act of grace; we are not only forgiven and healed, but <hi type="italic">preferred;</hi> there is a charter of privileges as well as pardon; and thus the Son makes us free <hi type="italic">denizens</hi> of the kingdom of priests, the holy nation, the new Jerusalem. <div eID="gen27377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27378" type="x-p"/> (2.) Those whom Christ makes free are <hi type="italic">free indeed.</hi> It is not <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">alethos</hi></hi>, the word used (<reference osisRef="John.8.31">v. 31</reference>) for disciples <hi type="italic">indeed, but</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ontos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">really.</hi> It denotes, [1.] The truth and certainty of the promise, the liberty which the Jews boasted of was an <hi type="italic">imaginary</hi> liberty; they boasted of a <hi type="italic">false gift;</hi> but the liberty which Christ gives is a certain thing, it is real, and has real effects. The servants of sin promise themselves liberty, and fancy themselves free, when they have broken religion's bands asunder; but they cheat themselves. None are <hi type="italic">free indeed</hi> but those whom Christ <hi type="italic">makes free.</hi> [2.] It denotes the singular excellency of the freedom promised; it is a freedom that deserves the name, in comparison with which all other liberties are no better than slaveries, so much does it turn to the honour and advantage of those that are <hi type="italic">made free</hi> by it. It is a <hi type="italic">glorious</hi> liberty. It is that which <hi type="italic">is</hi> (so <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ontos</hi></hi> signifies); it is <hi type="italic">substance</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.21">Prov. viii. 21</reference>); while the things of the world are shadows, things that <hi type="italic">are not.</hi> <div eID="gen27378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27379" type="x-p"/> 4. He applies this to these unbelieving cavilling Jews, in answer to their boasts of relation to Abraham (<reference osisRef="John.8.37">v. 37</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I know</hi> very well <hi type="italic">that you are Abraham's seed, but now you seek to kill me,</hi> and therefore have forfeited the honour of your relation to Abraham, <hi type="italic">because my word hath no place in you.</hi>" Observe here, <div eID="gen27379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27380" type="x-p"/> (1.) The dignity of their extraction admitted: "<hi type="italic">I know that you are Abraham's seed,</hi> every one knows it, and it is your honour." He grants them what was true, and in what they said that was false (that they were <hi type="italic">never</hi> in bondage to any) he does not <hi type="italic">contradict</hi> them, for he studied to <hi type="italic">profit</hi> them, and not to <hi type="italic">provoke</hi> them, and therefore said that which would please them: <hi type="italic">I know that you are Abraham's seed.</hi> They boasted of their descent from <hi type="italic">Abraham,</hi> as that which <hi type="italic">aggrandized</hi> their names, and made them exceedingly honourable; whereas really it did but <hi type="italic">aggravate</hi> their crimes, and make them exceedingly sinful. Out of their own mouths will he judge vain-glorious hypocrites, who boast of their parentage and education: "Are you Abraham's seed? Why then did you not tread in the steps of his faith and obedience?" <div eID="gen27380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27381" type="x-p"/> (2.) The inconsistency of their practice with this dignity: <hi type="italic">But you seek to kill me.</hi> They had attempted it several times, and were now designing it, which quickly appeared (<reference osisRef="John.8.59">v. 59</reference>), when they <hi type="italic">took up stones to cast at him.</hi> Christ knows all the wickedness, not only which men do, but which they seek, and design, and endeavour to do. To seek to kill any innocent man is a crime black enough, but to <hi type="italic">compass and imagine</hi> the death of him that was King of kings was a crime the heinousness of which we want words to express. <div eID="gen27381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27382" type="x-p"/> (3.) The reason of this inconsistency. Why were they that were Abraham's seed so very inveterate against Abraham's promised seed, in whom they and <hi type="italic">all the families of the earth</hi> should be <hi type="italic">blessed?</hi> Our Saviour here tells them, It is because <hi type="italic">my word hath no place in you,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ou chorei en hymin</hi></hi>, <hi type="italic">Non capit in vobis,</hi> so the Vulgate. "My word <hi type="italic">does not take with you,</hi> you have no inclination to it, no relish of it, other things are more taking, more pleasing." Or, "It does not <hi type="italic">take hold of you,</hi> it has no power over you, makes no impression upon you." Some of the critics read it, <hi type="italic">My word does not penetrate into you;</hi> it descended as the rain, but it came upon them as the rain upon the rock, which it runs off, and did not soak into their hearts, as the rain upon the ploughed ground. The Syriac reads it, "<hi type="italic">Because you do not acquiesce in my word;</hi> you are not persuaded of the truth of it, nor pleased with the goodness of it." Our translation is very significant: <hi type="italic">It has no place in you.</hi> They <hi type="italic">sought to kill him,</hi> and so effectually to <hi type="italic">silence</hi> him, not because he had done they any harm, but because they could not bear the convincing, commanding power of his word. Note, [1.] The words of Christ ought to have a place in us, the innermost and uppermost place,—a <hi type="italic">dwelling</hi> place, as a man at home, and not as a stranger or sojourner,—a <hi type="italic">working</hi> place; it must have room to operate, to work sin out of us, and to work grace in us; it must have a <hi type="italic">ruling</hi> place, its place must be <hi type="italic">upon the throne,</hi> it must dwell in us richly. [2.] There are many that make a profession of religion in whom <hi type="italic">the word of</hi> Christ has no place; they will not <hi type="italic">allow</hi> it a place, for they do not like it; Satan does all he can to <hi type="italic">displace</hi> it; and other things possess the place it should have in us. [3.] Where the word of God has no place no good is to be expected, for room is left there for all wickedness. If the unclean spirit find the heart empty of Christ's word, he <hi type="italic">enters in, and dwells there.</hi>
entries.b8271c0ee3ec82844e0f71c9cece968cec6c62c9: <div eID="gen27382" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Discourse with the Pharisees.</title> <div sID="gen27383" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">38</hi> I speak that which I have seen with my Father: and ye do that which ye have seen with your father. <hi type="super">39</hi> They answered and said unto him, Abraham is our father. Jesus saith unto them, If ye were Abraham's children, ye would do the works of Abraham. <hi type="super">40</hi> But now ye seek to kill me, a man that hath told you the truth, which I have heard of God: this did not Abraham. <hi type="super">41</hi> Ye do the deeds of your father. Then said they to him, We be not born of fornication; we have one Father, <hi type="italic">even</hi> God. <hi type="super">42</hi> Jesus said unto them, If God were your Father, ye would love me: for I proceeded forth and came from God; neither came I of myself, but he sent me. <hi type="super">43</hi> Why do ye not understand my speech? <hi type="italic">even</hi> because ye cannot hear my word. 44 Ye are of <hi type="italic">your</hi> father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do. He was a murderer from the beginning, and abode not in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it. <hi type="super">45</hi> And because I tell <hi type="italic">you</hi> the truth, ye believe me not. <hi type="super">46</hi> Which of you convinceth me of sin? And if I say the truth, why do ye not believe me? <hi type="super">47</hi> He that is of God heareth God's words: ye therefore hear <hi type="italic">them</hi> not, because ye are not of God. <div eID="gen27383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27384" type="x-p"/> Here Christ and the Jews are still at issue; he sets himself to convince and convert them, while they still set themselves to contradict and oppose him. <div eID="gen27384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27385" type="x-p"/> I. He here traces the difference between his sentiments and theirs to a different rise and origin (<reference osisRef="John.8.38">v. 38</reference>): <hi type="italic">I speak that which I have seen with my Father,</hi> and <hi type="italic">you</hi> do <hi type="italic">what you have seen with your father.</hi> Here are two fathers spoken of, according to the two families into which the sons of men are divided—God and the devil, and without controversy these are contrary the one to the other. <div eID="gen27385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27386" type="x-p"/> 1. Christ's <hi type="italic">doctrine</hi> was from <hi type="italic">heaven;</hi> it was <hi type="italic">copied</hi> out of the <hi type="italic">counsels</hi> of infinite wisdom, and the kind intentions of eternal love. (1.) <hi type="italic">I speak that which I have seen.</hi> The discoveries Christ has made to us of God and another world are not grounded upon guess and hearsay, but upon ocular inspection; so that he was thoroughly <hi type="italic">apprized</hi> of the nature, and <hi type="italic">assured</hi> of the truth, of all he said. He that is given to be a witness to the people is an eye-witness, and therefore unexceptionable. (2.) It is what I have seen <hi type="italic">with my Father.</hi> The doctrine of Christ is not a plausible hypothesis, supported by probable arguments, but it is an exact counterpart of the incontestable truths lodged in the eternal mind. It was not only what he had <hi type="italic">heard from</hi> his Father, but what he had <hi type="italic">seen with him</hi> when <hi type="italic">the counsel of peace was between them both.</hi> Moses spoke what he heard from God, but he might not see the face of God; Paul had been in the third heaven, but what he had seen there he could not, he must not, utter; for it was Christ's prerogative to have <hi type="italic">seen</hi> what he <hi type="italic">spoke,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">speak</hi> what he had <hi type="italic">seen.</hi> <div eID="gen27386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27387" type="x-p"/> 2. Their <hi type="italic">doings</hi> were from hell: "<hi type="italic">You do that which you have seen with your father.</hi> You do, by your own works, father yourselves, for it is evident whom you resemble, and therefore easy to find out your origin." As a child that is trained up with his father learns his father's words and fashions, and grows like him by an affected imitation as well as by a natural image, so these Jews, by their malicious opposition to Christ and the gospel, made themselves as like the devil as if they had industriously set him before them for their pattern. <div eID="gen27387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27388" type="x-p"/> II. He takes off and answers their vain-glorious boasts of relation to Abraham and to God as their fathers, and shows the vanity and falsehood of their pretensions. <div eID="gen27388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27389" type="x-p"/> 1. They pleaded relation to Abraham, and he replies to this plea. <hi type="italic">They said, Abraham is our father,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.8.39">v. 39</reference>. In this they intended, (1.) To do honour to themselves, and to make themselves look great. They had forgotten the mortification given them by that acknowledgement prescribed them (<reference osisRef="Deut.26.5">Deut. xxvi. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">A Syrian ready to perish was my father;</hi> and the charge exhibited against their degenerate ancestors (whose steps they trod in, and not those of the first founder of the family), <hi type="italic">Thy father was an Amorite, and thy mother a Hittite,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.3">Ezek. xvi. 3</reference>. As it is common for those families that are sinking and going to decay to boast most of their pedigree, so it is common for those churches that are corrupt and depraved to value themselves upon their antiquity and the eminence of their first planters. <hi type="italic">Fuimus Troes, fuit Ilium—We have been Trojans, and there once was Troy.</hi> (2.) They designed to cast an odium upon Christ as if he reflected upon the patriarch Abraham, in speaking of their father as one they had learned evil from. See how they sought an occasion to quarrel with him. Now Christ overthrows this plea, and exposes the vanity of it by a plain and cogent argument: "Abraham's children will do the works of Abraham, but you do not do Abraham's works, therefore you are not Abraham's children." <div eID="gen27389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27390" type="x-p"/> [1.] The proposition is plain: "<hi type="italic">If you were Abraham's children,</hi> such children of Abraham as could claim an interest in the covenant made with him and his seed, which would indeed put an honour upon you, then you would <hi type="italic">do the works of Abraham,</hi> for to those only of Abraham's house who <hi type="italic">kept the way of the Lord,</hi> as Abraham did, would God <hi type="italic">perform what he had spoken,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Gen.18.19">Gen. xviii. 19</reference>. Those only are reckoned the seed of Abraham, to whom the promise belongs, who <hi type="italic">tread in the steps</hi> of his faith and obedience, <reference osisRef="Rom.4.12">Rom. iv. 12</reference>. Though the Jews had their genealogies, and kept them exact, yet they could not by them make out their relation to Abraham, so as to take the benefit of the old entail (<hi type="italic">performam doni—according to the form of the gift</hi>), unless they walked in the same spirit; good women's relation to Sarah is proved only by this—<hi type="italic">whose daughters you are as long as you do well,</hi> and no longer, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.6">1 Pet. iii. 6</reference>. Note, Those who would approve themselves Abraham's seed must not only be of Abraham's faith, but do Abraham's works (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.21-Jas.2.22">James ii. 21, 22</reference>),—must come at God's call, as he did,—must resign their dearest comforts to him,—must be strangers and sojourners in this world,—must keep up the worship of God in their families, and always walk before God in their uprightness; for these were the works of Abraham. <div eID="gen27390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27391" type="x-p"/> [2.] The assumption is evident likewise: <hi type="italic">But you do not do</hi> the works of Abraham, for <hi type="italic">you seek to kill me, a man that has told you the truth, which I have heard of God; this did not Abraham,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.8.40">v. 40</reference>. <div eID="gen27391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27392" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He shows them what their work was, their present work, which they were now about; they <hi type="italic">sought to kill him;</hi> and three things are intimated as an aggravation of their intention:—1. They were so <hi type="italic">unnatural</hi> as to seek the life of <hi type="italic">a man,</hi> a man like themselves, bone of their bone, and flesh of their flesh, who had done them no harm, nor given them any provocation. You <hi type="italic">imagine mischief against a man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.62.3">Ps. lxii. 3</reference>. 2. They were so <hi type="italic">ungrateful</hi> as to seek the life of one who had <hi type="italic">told them the truth,</hi> had not only done them no injury, but had done them the greatest kindness that could be; had not only not imposed upon them with a lie, but had instructed them in the most necessary and important truths; <hi type="italic">was he therefore become their enemy?</hi> 3. They were so <hi type="italic">ungodly</hi> as to seek the life of one who told them the truth <hi type="italic">which he had heard from God,</hi> who was a messenger sent from God to them, so that their attempt against him was <hi type="italic">quasi deicidium—an act of malice against God.</hi> This was their work, and they persisted in it. <div eID="gen27392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27393" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He shows them that this did not become the children of Abraham; for <hi type="italic">this did not Abraham.</hi> 1. "He did nothing like this." He was famous for his humanity, witness his rescue of the captives; and for his piety, witness his obedience to the heavenly vision in many instances, and some tender ones. Abraham believed God; they were obstinate in unbelief: Abraham followed God; they fought against him; so that he would be <hi type="italic">ignorant of them, and would not acknowledge them,</hi> they were so unlike him, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.16">Isa. lxiii. 16</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Jer.22.15-Jer.22.17">Jer. xxii. 15-17</reference>. 2. "He would not have done thus if he had lived now, or I had lived then." <hi type="italic">Hoc Abraham non fecisset—He would not have done this;</hi> so some read it. We should thus reason ourselves out of any way of wickedness; would Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob have done so? We cannot expect to be <hi type="italic">ever with them,</hi> if we be <hi type="italic">never like them.</hi> <div eID="gen27393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27394" type="x-p"/> [3.] The conclusion follows of course (<reference osisRef="John.8.41">v. 41</reference>): "Whatever your boasts and pretensions be, you are not Abraham's children, but father yourselves upon another family (<reference osisRef="John.8.41">v. 41</reference>); there is <hi type="italic">a father whose deeds you do,</hi> whose spirit you are of, and whom you resemble." He does not <hi type="italic">yet</hi> say plainly that he means the devil, till they by their continued cavils forced him so to explain himself, which teaches us to treat even bad men with civility and respect, and not to be forward to say that <hi type="italic">of</hi> them, or <hi type="italic">to</hi> them, which, though <hi type="italic">true,</hi> sounds <hi type="italic">harsh.</hi> He tried whether they would suffer their own consciences to infer from what he said that they were the devil's children; and it is better to hear it from them now that we are called to <hi type="italic">repent,</hi> that is, to change our father and change our family, by changing our spirit and way, than to hear it from Christ in the great day. <div eID="gen27394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27395" type="x-p"/> 2. So far were they from owning their unworthiness of relation to Abraham that they pleaded relation to God himself as their Father: "We are <hi type="italic">not born of fornication,</hi> we are not bastards, but legitimate sons; <hi type="italic">we have one Father, even God.</hi>" <div eID="gen27395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27396" type="x-p"/> (1.) Some understand this literally. They were not the sons of the bondwoman, as the Ishmaelites were; nor begotten in incest, as the Moabites and Ammonites were (<reference osisRef="Deut.23.3">Deut. xxiii. 3</reference>); nor were they a spurious brood in Abraham's family, but Hebrews of the Hebrews; and, being born in <hi type="italic">lawful</hi> wedlock, they might call God <hi type="italic">Father,</hi> who instituted that honourable estate in innocency; for a legitimate seed, not tainted with divorces nor the plurality of wives, is called a <hi type="italic">seed of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.2.15">Mal. ii. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen27396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27397" type="x-p"/> (2.) Others take it figuratively. They begin to be aware now that Christ spoke of a <hi type="italic">spiritual</hi> not a <hi type="italic">carnal</hi> father, of the father of their religion; and so, <div eID="gen27397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27398" type="x-p"/> [1.] They deny themselves to be a generation of idolaters: "We are <hi type="italic">not born of fornication,</hi> are not the children of idolatrous parents, nor have been bred up in idolatrous worships." Idolatry is often spoken of as spiritual <hi type="italic">whoredom,</hi> and idolaters as <hi type="italic">children of whoredoms,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.2.4">Hosea ii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.3">Isa. lvii. 3</reference>. Now, if they meant that they were not the posterity of idolaters, the allegation was false, for no nation was more addicted to idolatry than the Jews before the captivity; if they meant no more than that they themselves were not idolaters, what then? A man may be free from idolatry, and yet perish in another iniquity, and be shut out of Abraham's covenant. <hi type="italic">If thou commit no idolatry</hi> (apply it to this spiritual fornication), yet if thou kill thou art become a <hi type="italic">transgressor</hi> of the covenant. A rebellious prodigal son will be disinherited, though he be not <hi type="italic">born of fornication.</hi> <div eID="gen27398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27399" type="x-p"/> [2.] They boast themselves to be true worshippers of the true God. We have not many fathers, as the heathens had, <hi type="italic">gods many and lords many,</hi> and yet were without God, as <hi type="italic">filius populi—a son of the people,</hi> has many fathers and yet none certain; no, <hi type="italic">the Lord our God is one Lord</hi> and <hi type="italic">one Father,</hi> and therefore it is well with us. Note, Those flatter themselves, and put a damning cheat upon their own souls, who imagine that their professing the true religion and worshipping the true God will save them, though they worship not God in spirit and in truth, nor are true to their profession. Now our Saviour gives a full answer to this fallacious plea (<reference osisRef="John.8.42-John.8.43">v. 42, 43</reference>), and proves, by two arguments, that they had no right to call God Father. <div eID="gen27399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27400" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They did not love Christ: <hi type="italic">If God were your Father, you would love me.</hi> He had disproved their relation to Abraham by their going about to kill him (<reference osisRef="John.8.40">v. 40</reference>), but here he disproves their relation to God by their not loving and owning him. A man may pass for a <hi type="italic">child</hi> of Abraham if he do not appear an enemy to Christ by gross sin; but he cannot approve himself a child of God unless he be a faithful friend and follower of Christ. Note, All that have God for their Father have a true love to Jesus Christ, and esteem of his person, a grateful sense of his love, a sincere affection to his cause and kingdom, a complacency in the salvation wrought out by him and in the method and terms of it, and a care to keep his commandments, which is the surest evidence of our love to him. We are here in a state of probation, upon our trial how we will conduct ourselves towards our Maker, and accordingly it will be with us in the state of retribution. God has taken various methods to prove us, and this was one: he sent his Son into the world, with sufficient proofs of his sonship and mission, concluding that all that called him Father would <hi type="italic">kiss his Son,</hi> and bid <hi type="italic">him</hi> welcome who was the first-born among many brethren; see <reference osisRef="1John.5.1">1 John v. 1</reference>. By this our adoption will be proved or disproved—Did we love Christ, or no? <hi type="italic">If any man do not,</hi> he is so far from being a child of God that he is <hi type="italic">anathema,</hi> accursed, <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.22">1 Cor. xvi. 22</reference>. Now our Saviour proves that if they were God's children they would <hi type="italic">love him;</hi> for, saith he, I proceeded <hi type="italic">forth and came from God.</hi> They will love him; for, 1. He was the <hi type="italic">Son of God: I proceeded forth from God.</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Exelthon</hi></hi> this means his divine <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">exeleusis</hi></hi>, or origin from the Father, by the communication of the divine essence, and also the union of the divine <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">logos</hi></hi> to his human nature; so Dr. Whitby. Now this could not but recommend him to the affections of all that were <hi type="italic">born of God.</hi> Christ is called the <hi type="italic">beloved,</hi> because, being the beloved of the Father, he is certainly the beloved of all the saints, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.6">Eph. i. 6</reference>. 2. He was <hi type="italic">sent of God,</hi> came from him as an ambassador to the world of mankind. He did not <hi type="italic">come of himself,</hi> as the false prophets, who had not either their <hi type="italic">mission</hi> or their <hi type="italic">message</hi> from God, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.21">Jer. xxiii. 21</reference>. Observe the emphasis he lays upon this: <hi type="italic">I came from God; neither came I of myself, but he sent me.</hi> He had both his credentials and his instructions from God; he came to <hi type="italic">gather together in one the children of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.11.51">ch. xi. 51</reference>), to bring <hi type="italic">many sons to glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.2.10">Heb. ii. 10</reference>. And would not all God's children embrace with both arms a messenger sent from their Father on <hi type="italic">such</hi> errands? But these Jews made it appear that they were nothing akin to God, by their want of affection to Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen27400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27401" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They did not understand him. It was a sign they did not belong to God's family that they did not understand the language and dialect of the family: <hi type="italic">You do not understand my speech</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.8.43">v. 43</reference>), <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ten lalian ten emen</hi></hi>. Christ's speech was divine and heavenly, but intelligible enough to those that were acquainted with the voice of Christ in the Old Testament. Those that had made the word of the Creator familiar to them needed no other key to the dialect of the Redeemer; and yet these Jews make strange of the doctrine of Christ, and find knots in it, and I know not what stumbling stones. Could a Galilean be known by his speech? An Ephraimite by his <hi type="italic">sibboleth?</hi> And would any have the confidence to call God Father to whom the Son of God was a barbarian, even when he spoke the will of God in the words of the Spirit of God? Note, Those who are not acquainted with the divine speech have reason to fear that they are strangers to the divine nature. Christ spoke the words of God (<reference osisRef="John.3.34">ch. iii. 34</reference>) in the dialect of the kingdom of God; and yet they, who pretended to belong to the kingdom, understood not the idioms and properties of it, but like strangers, and rude ones too, ridiculed it. And the reason why they did not understand Christ's speech made the matter much worse: <hi type="italic">Even because you cannot hear my word,</hi> that is, "You cannot persuade yourselves to hear it attentively, impartially, and without prejudice, as it should be heard." The meaning of this <hi type="italic">cannot</hi> is an obstinate <hi type="italic">will not;</hi> as the Jews could not hear Stephen (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.57">Acts vii. 57</reference>) nor Paul, <reference osisRef="Acts.23.22">Acts xxiii. 22</reference>. Note, The rooted antipathy of men's corrupt hearts to the doctrine of Christ is the true reason of their ignorance of it, and of their errors and mistakes about it. They do not like it nor love it, and therefore they will not understand it; like Peter, who pretended he <hi type="italic">knew not what the damsel said</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.70">Matt. xxvi. 70</reference>), when in truth he knew not what to say to it. <hi type="italic">You cannot hear my words,</hi> for you have <hi type="italic">stopped your ears</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.58.4-Ps.58.5">Ps. lviii. 4, 5</reference>), and God, in a way of righteous judgment, <hi type="italic">has made your ears heavy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.6.10">Isa. vi. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen27401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27402" type="x-p"/> III. Having thus disproved their relation both to Abraham and to God, he comes next to tell them plainly whose children they were: <hi type="italic">You are of your father the devil,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.8.44">v. 44</reference>. If they were not God's children, they were the devil's, for God and Satan divide the world of mankind; the devil is <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> said to <hi type="italic">work in the children of disobedience,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.2">Eph. ii. 2</reference>. All wicked people are the devil's children, <hi type="italic">children of Belial</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.6.15">2 Cor. vi. 15</reference>), the serpent's seed (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Gen. iii. 15</reference>), children of the wicked one, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.38">Matt. xiii. 38</reference>. They partake of his nature, bear his image, obey his commands, and follow his example. Idolaters <hi type="italic">said to a stock, Thou art our father,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.2.27">Jer. ii. 27</reference>. <div eID="gen27402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27403" type="x-p"/> This is a high charge, and sounds very harsh and horrid, that any of the children of men, especially the church's children, should be called <hi type="italic">children of the devil,</hi> and therefore our Saviour fully proves it. <div eID="gen27403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27404" type="x-p"/> 1. By a general argument: <hi type="italic">The lusts of your father you will do,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">thelete poiein</hi></hi>. (1.) "You <hi type="italic">do</hi> the devil's lusts, the lusts which he would have you to fulfil; you gratify and please him, and comply with his temptation, and are <hi type="italic">led captive by him at his will:</hi> nay, you do those lusts which the devil himself fulfils." Fleshly lusts and worldly lusts the devil tempts men to; but, being a spirit, he cannot fulfil them himself. The peculiar lusts of the devil are <hi type="italic">spiritual wickedness;</hi> the lusts of the intellectual powers, and their corrupt reasonings; pride and envy, and wrath and malice; enmity to that which is good, and enticing others to that which is evil; these are lusts which the devil fulfils, and those who are under the dominion of these lusts resemble the devil, as the child does the parent. The more there is of contemplation, and contrivance, and secret complacency, in sin, the more it resembles the <hi type="italic">lusts of the devil.</hi> (2.) You <hi type="italic">will do</hi> the devil's lusts. The more there is of the <hi type="italic">will</hi> in these lusts, the more there is of the devil in them. When sin is committed <hi type="italic">of choice</hi> and not by surprise, with <hi type="italic">pleasure</hi> and not with reluctancy, when it is persisted in with a daring presumption and a desperate resolution, like theirs that said, <hi type="italic">We have loved strangers and after them we will go,</hi> then the sinner <hi type="italic">will</hi> do the devil's lusts. "The lusts of your father you <hi type="italic">delight to do;</hi>" so Dr. Hammond; they are rolled under the tongue as a sweet morsel. <div eID="gen27404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27405" type="x-p"/> 2. By two particular instances, wherein they manifestly resembled the devil—<hi type="italic">murder</hi> and <hi type="italic">lying.</hi> The devil is an enemy to life, because God is the God of life and life is the happiness of man; and an enemy to truth, because God is the God of truth and truth is the bond of human society. <div eID="gen27405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27406" type="x-p"/> (1.) He was <hi type="italic">a murderer from the beginning,</hi> not from his own beginning, for he was created an angel of light, and had a first estate which was pure and good, but from the beginning of his apostasy, which was soon after the creation of man. He was <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">anthropoktonos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">homicida, a man-slayer.</hi> [1.] He was a <hi type="italic">hater of man,</hi> and so in affection an disposition a murderer of him. He has his name, <hi type="italic">Satan,</hi> from <hi type="italic">sitnah—hatred.</hi> He maligned God's image upon man, envied his happiness, and earnestly desired his ruin, was an avowed enemy to the whole race. [2.] He was man's tempter to <hi type="italic">that</hi> sin which brought death into the world, and so he was effectually the murderer of all mankind, which in Adam had but <hi type="italic">one neck.</hi> He was a murderer of souls, <hi type="italic">deceived</hi> them into sin, and by it <hi type="italic">slew them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.11">Rom. vii. 11</reference>), poisoned man with the forbidden fruit, and, to aggravate the matter, made him his own murderer. Thus he was not only <hi type="italic">at</hi> the beginning, but <hi type="italic">from</hi> the beginning, which intimates that thus he <hi type="italic">has been</hi> ever since; as he began, so he continues, the murderer of men by his temptations. The great tempter is the great destroyer. The Jews called the devil <hi type="italic">the angel of death.</hi> [3.] He was the first wheel in the first murder that ever was committed by Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother, <reference osisRef="1John.3.12">1 John iii. 12</reference>. If the devil had not been very strong in Cain, he could not have done such an unnatural thing as to kill his own brother. Cain killing his brother by the instigation of the devil, the devil is called the <hi type="italic">murderer,</hi> which does not speak Cain's personal guilt the less, but the devil's the more, whose torments, we have reason to think, will be the greater, when the time comes, for all that wickedness into which he has drawn men. See what reason we have to <hi type="italic">stand</hi> upon our guard <hi type="italic">against the wiles of the devil,</hi> and never to hearken to him (for he is a murderer, and certainly aims to do us mischief, even when he <hi type="italic">speaks fair</hi>), and to wonder that he who is the murderer of the children of men should yet be, by their own consent, so much their master. Now herein these Jews were followers of him, and were murderers, like him; murderers of souls, which they led blindfold into the ditch, and made the <hi type="italic">children of hell;</hi> sworn enemies of Christ, and now ready to be his betrayers and murderers, for the same reason that Cain killed Abel. These Jews were that <hi type="italic">seed of the serpent</hi> that were to <hi type="italic">bruise the heel</hi> of the <hi type="italic">seed of the woman; Now you seek to kill me.</hi> <div eID="gen27406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27407" type="x-p"/> (2.) He was <hi type="italic">a liar.</hi> A lie is opposed to truth (<reference osisRef="1John.2.21">1 John ii. 21</reference>), and accordingly the devil is here described to be, <div eID="gen27407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27408" type="x-p"/> [1.] An enemy to truth, and therefore to Christ. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He is a <hi type="italic">deserter,</hi> from the truth; he <hi type="italic">abode not in the truth,</hi> did not continue in the purity and rectitude of his nature wherein he was created, but left his first state; when he degenerated from goodness, he departed from truth, for his apostasy was founded in a lie. The angels were the <hi type="italic">hosts of the Lord;</hi> those that fell were not <hi type="italic">true</hi> to their commander and sovereign, they were not to be <hi type="italic">trusted,</hi> being charged with folly and defection, <reference osisRef="Job.4.18">Job iv. 18</reference>. By <hi type="italic">the truth</hi> here we may understand the revealed will of God concerning the salvation of man by Jesus Christ, the truth which Christ was now preaching, and which the Jews opposed; herein they did <hi type="italic">like their father the devil,</hi> who, <hi type="italic">seeing</hi> the honour put upon the human nature in the <hi type="italic">first Adam,</hi> and <hi type="italic">foreseeing</hi> the much greater honour intended in the <hi type="italic">second Adam,</hi> would not be reconciled to that counsel of God, nor <hi type="italic">stand in the truth</hi> concerning it, but, from a spirit of pride and envy, set himself to resist it, and to thwart the designs of it; and so did these Jews here, as his children and agents. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He is <hi type="italic">destitute</hi> of the truth: <hi type="italic">There is no truth in him.</hi> His interest in the world is supported by lies and falsehoods, and there is no truth, nothing you can confide in, in him, nor in any thing he says or does. The notions he propagates concerning good and evil are false and erroneous, his proofs are lying wonders, his temptations are all cheats; he has great knowledge of the truth, but having no affection to it, but on the contrary being a sworn enemy to it, he is said to have <hi type="italic">no truth in him.</hi> <div eID="gen27408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27409" type="x-p"/> [2.] He is a friend and patron of lying: <hi type="italic">When he speaketh a lie he speaketh of his own.</hi> Three things are here said of the devil with reference to the sin of lying:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> That he is <hi type="italic">a liar;</hi> his oracles were lying oracles, his prophets lying prophets, and the images in which he was worshipped <hi type="italic">teachers of lies.</hi> He tempted our first parents with a downright lie. All his temptations are carried on by lies, calling <hi type="italic">evil good and good evil,</hi> and promising impunity in sin; he knows them to be lies, and suggests them with an intention to deceive, and so to destroy.
